references_named: Roger de Piles, Balance des Peintres / Cours de peinture par principes (1708)
rationale: The mechanism is genuinely the argument: native <meter> with low/high/optimum is spec-obliged to color itself green or red, so the aesthetic verdict is authored by the browser vendor, not the file. This is a clean digital readymade (de Piles's table + the HTML gauge primitive snapped together) that sits squarely on the order pole of the chance/order axis and targets value/canonization. Double-coding works: a casual viewer sees colored bars grading Old Masters; a literate viewer gets the Enlightenment's dream of measurable taste and its rating-economy afterlife. Restraint is exemplary — zero JS, smallest possible build, attribution and license stated.
reservations: Novelty is real but the <meter>-as-verdict move is a recognizable net.art trope (browser chrome as material); the piece earns its place by the specific historical pairing with de Piles rather than by inventing the technique. The work is static — no live/regenerating behavior beyond the per-vendor rendering — which slightly undercuts P4, though the vendor-drawn verdict is itself a form of per-visit variation.
revision_suggestion: Consider a tiny per-visit perturbation (e.g., a CSS custom property seeded from the visit that nudges the low/high thresholds by ±1) so the same painter can flip green/red across reloads, making the 'taste is nobody's' point literally unstable rather than only vendor-dependent.
